title: CROSS JOIN
description: Generate deliberate SQL combinations with CROSS JOIN, predict result sizes, preserve missing combinations for reporting, and avoid accidental Cartesian multiplication.
notes:
## Combine every row with every other row

CROSS JOIN forms the Cartesian product of two row sources. Every row from the first source is paired with every row from the second. If a campus workshop offers three dates and two rooms, their cross join describes six date-room combinations. It does not say that a booking exists for any combination, that the room is available, or that every combination should be offered. It establishes a candidate space on which later rules can operate.

This operation is useful when the requirement truly begins with all combinations. It is dangerous when an intended relationship predicate has simply been forgotten. Start with [join cardinality](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-cardinality) and [INNER JOIN](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/inner-join) if matching rows by a key is still unfamiliar. The choice between matching existing relationships and generating possibilities should be explicit in the report specification.

## Trace a two-by-three product

Suppose two workshop formats can be offered in three slots. Each source row has a stable identifier, so identical display labels remain distinguishable. The output grain is one format-slot pair. Use qualified column names and choose the intended output columns rather than allowing SELECT star to obscure repeated identifiers from both sources.

```sql
CREATE TABLE formats (
  format_id INT PRIMARY KEY, format_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE slots (
  slot_id INT PRIMARY KEY, starts_at TIME NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO formats VALUES (1,'Intro'),(2,'Practice');
INSERT INTO slots VALUES (10,'09:00:00'),(20,'11:00:00'),(30,'14:00:00');

SELECT f.format_id, s.slot_id
FROM formats AS f CROSS JOIN slots AS s
ORDER BY f.format_id, s.slot_id;
```

The six pairs are 1 with 10, 20 and 30, followed by 2 with 10, 20 and 30. No equality predicate is needed because every pairing is intentional. The ORDER BY is still needed for that display sequence. A Cartesian product has no inherent row order, even if one small execution happens to return nested-loop-looking output.

The count rule multiplies source row counts, including repeated source rows. Two rows crossed with three rows yield six, even if some projected labels look identical. If either source contains zero rows, the product has zero rows. A source with exactly one row can attach a single configuration value to every row of another source, provided that its one-row contract is actually enforced.

## Keep SQL bags separate from mathematical sets

Relational algebra often introduces a Cartesian product over sets. SQL query results can contain duplicates. Two different format identifiers may share the name Intro, and two distinct slots may share the same displayed time. Selecting only names and times can therefore produce visually repeated combinations without the join having duplicated any source identity. Preserve identifiers until the desired output grain is clear.

DISTINCT can collapse equal projected combinations, but that changes the question from which source pairs exist to which displayed value combinations exist. It may be exactly what a report asks, or it may conceal valid distinctions. Do not add DISTINCT simply because a large Cartesian result looks repetitive. Check whether the input dimensions themselves are supposed to be unique at the chosen business key.

## Filter candidates with an explicit compatibility rule

A cross join can generate candidate assignments followed by a condition that removes incompatible pairs. For example, a workshop format needing forty seats can be paired with rooms and then filtered to rooms whose capacity is sufficient. The surviving set is no longer the complete Cartesian product, but the all-pairs starting model can still explain the requirement.

```sql
SELECT f.format_id, r.room_id
FROM required_formats AS f
CROSS JOIN rooms AS r
WHERE r.capacity >= f.required_seats
ORDER BY f.format_id, r.room_id;
```

A non-equality INNER JOIN with the same condition expresses the same matching rule. Prefer the form that makes the business intent easiest to review. MySQL treats CROSS JOIN and INNER JOIN as syntactic equivalents in its join grammar, but writing CROSS JOIN without a matching condition makes the all-pairs intention visible and travels more clearly across dialects. Do not infer a required physical materialization from the written syntax.

Filtering a dimension before combination can shrink the candidate space. If the report only includes active rooms, make that eligibility clear. An optimizer may move safe predicates, choose indexes or change join order. Those decisions do not excuse an unbounded product in an application feature. Estimate the requested result size and constrain user-controlled date ranges or dimension selections at the trusted request boundary.

## Build a complete reporting grid

A daily attendance report may need every requested date for every active workshop, including combinations with no attendance facts. Starting from attendance alone cannot produce a workshop-date pair that has no row. Cross the selected workshops with the selected dates, then LEFT JOIN preaggregated attendance at exactly that pair grain. This creates the reporting population before adding observed measures.

```sql
SELECT w.workshop_id, d.report_date,
       COALESCE(a.attendee_count,0) AS attendee_count
FROM workshops AS w
CROSS JOIN report_dates AS d
LEFT JOIN attendance_totals AS a
  ON a.workshop_id = w.workshop_id
 AND a.report_date = d.report_date
ORDER BY w.workshop_id, d.report_date;
```

The attendance totals source must have at most one row per workshop and date. Otherwise one candidate pair becomes several result rows. The zero replacement is a reporting policy: it assumes no matching attendance fact means zero attendees, rather than an uncollected or unavailable measurement. If the system distinguishes those states, retain a completeness flag and avoid presenting missing evidence as a measured zero.

A filter on right-side attendance columns in WHERE can discard null-extended rows and undo the complete-grid requirement. Put match eligibility in the appropriate ON condition or preaggregation, and test an entirely empty attendance source. See [LEFT JOIN](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/left-join) for the preservation behavior that makes this pattern work.

## Recognize accidental products in ordinary joins

Suppose orders have several items and several tags. Joining items and tags independently by order identifier can produce every item-tag pair within each order. This is a local Cartesian multiplication even though each join has a plausible key predicate. Summing item amounts afterward repeats each amount once per tag. The defect is about grain, not merely whether the keyword CROSS appears.

Preaggregate each one-to-many source to the intended order grain, or use an existence check when tags only decide eligibility. A missing relationship predicate between two wholly unrelated tables is another common cause. Debug multiplication by selecting source identifiers and counting rows per intended fact identity before calculating final measures. A larger-than-expected sum is often the first visible symptom of an earlier pairing error.

## Pair a table with itself carefully

Cross joining two aliases of the same table generates all ordered pairs, including a row with itself. With four distinct members, that is sixteen pairs. If the requirement is every unordered pair of different members, a condition such as first identifier less than second identifier excludes self-pairs and avoids emitting both directions. The result then has six pairs, provided the identifiers are unique and non-null.

The inequality is a symmetry-breaking rule, not a test that one member is more eligible than another. If pair direction has meaning, such as sender and recipient, removing reverse pairs changes the requirement. Describe whether self-pairs and direction are allowed before adopting a familiar pairing formula. Extend the fixtures with duplicate display names so that pairing remains based on identity.

A singleton configuration source should also have an explicit empty-input policy. If no configuration row exists, crossing it with valid events silently yields no events. If several configuration rows exist, every event repeats. A scalar setting lookup or a separately validated configuration contract may describe that requirement more clearly than assuming the configuration table is always populated exactly once.

## Bound and verify the intended combination space

Three dimensions multiply just as two do. Twenty workshops, thirty dates and ten rooms already describe six thousand candidate combinations. Large results consume memory, transfer bandwidth and rendering time even if the database finds an efficient execution plan. LIMIT can cap displayed output but does not necessarily make the underlying calculation cheap or produce a representative sample.

Test a normal product, one empty dimension, a singleton configuration source and repeated labels with distinct identifiers. For a reporting grid, add a missing fact and a duplicated fact key. For pair generation, test self-pair exclusion and both directions. A successful explanation can name exactly what one output row represents and predict its count before SQL runs; that is the strongest first defense against accidental multiplication.

questions.question_text: What does CROSS JOIN produce?
options: Only matched rows between two tables
Every possible combination of rows from both tables (a Cartesian Product)
Only rows from the first table
An error, since no join condition is given
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN explicitly requests the full Cartesian Product.

questions.question_text: With 4 employees and 3 departments, how many rows does CROSS JOIN produce?
questions.explanation: The row count is the product of the two table sizes: 4 x 3 = 12.

questions.question_text: For an intentional complete Cartesian product, does CROSS JOIN need an ON predicate?
options: Yes, always
No; omit a matching predicate to express all pairs. MySQL additionally permits ON because its CROSS JOIN and INNER JOIN grammar overlap
Only if the tables share a column name
ON is optional but recommended
questions.explanation: An unconditional CROSS JOIN expresses every pair without ON. MySQL permits conditions in its CROSS JOIN syntax, so claiming every ON clause is a syntax error would be incorrect.

questions.question_text: Which older FROM syntax unconditionally forms every pair when no WHERE filter is supplied?
options: FROM a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.id
FROM a, b (comma-separated) with no WHERE condition
SELECT * FROM a UNION b
FROM a INTERSECT b
questions.explanation: A comma-separated FROM list without a relationship filter forms the product. A conditional INNER JOIN restricts pairs; MySQL also accepts a bare JOIN without ON, so that cannot be used as a false alternative.

questions.question_text: What is a genuinely useful, deliberate application of CROSS JOIN?
options: Finding matching rows between two tables
Generating combinations, like every date crossed with every store, as a base for a reporting query
Removing duplicate rows
Sorting a table's rows
questions.explanation: Deliberately generating a full combination set is a real, common use case, unlike the accidental version.

questions.question_text: What is a real risk of using CROSS JOIN on two large tables?
options: No risk — CROSS JOIN is always efficient
The row count explosion (product of both sizes) can produce an enormous, resource-exhausting result even from moderately sized tables
CROSS JOIN always fails on tables larger than 100 rows
CROSS JOIN automatically limits its own output
questions.explanation: This mirrors the same row-count risk covered for Cartesian Product in relational algebra (7.7).

questions.question_text: Is explicit CROSS JOIN syntax generally considered better practice than the old comma-separated FROM style?
options: No, they are equally good
Yes — explicit CROSS JOIN makes the intent to produce every combination clear and deliberate, rather than looking like a forgotten join condition
The comma-separated style is always preferred
Both styles are deprecated in modern SQL
questions.explanation: Explicitness about intent is exactly why CROSS JOIN is favored over the ambiguous old-style comma syntax.

questions.question_text: Can CROSS JOIN be combined with a WHERE clause afterward?
options: No, WHERE cannot follow CROSS JOIN
Yes; logically WHERE keeps qualifying pairs, while the optimizer may avoid materializing the full product
WHERE automatically converts CROSS JOIN into INNER JOIN with no visible syntax change
CROSS JOIN ignores any WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Filtering a product is a logical description. An optimizer can apply safe conditions during access and join execution.

questions.question_text: How many rows are in a complete product of 4 and 7 source rows?
questions.explanation: Every first-source row pairs with every second-source row.

questions.question_text: What happens when one CROSS JOIN input is empty?
options: The other input is returned unchanged
One NULL row is added automatically
The result is empty
The statement must fail
questions.explanation: There are no possible pairs when either side has no rows.

questions.question_text: Does CROSS JOIN establish room availability?
options: Yes, automatically
Only for rooms with an index
Only when ordered by identifier
No, it only constructs candidate pairs
questions.explanation: Availability requires its own facts and conditions.

questions.question_text: Why preserve source identifiers while debugging combinations?
options: Equal labels may represent distinct source rows
Identifiers force an ordered result
Labels can never repeat
CROSS JOIN rejects text
questions.explanation: Projected equality does not imply duplicate source identity.

questions.question_text: Which join adds observed measures while keeping every candidate grid pair?
options: INNER JOIN from measures to the grid
LEFT JOIN from the grid to measures
A WHERE condition rejecting missing measures
UNION that removes all NULLs
questions.explanation: The left side defines the complete reporting population.

questions.question_text: What must attendance_totals guarantee for a one-row-per-workshop-date grid?
options: Only one row in the entire table
No numeric values
At most one row per workshop and date
At least two rows per key
questions.explanation: Duplicate measure keys multiply a grid pair.

questions.question_text: What does COALESCE of missing attendance to zero assume?
options: The source was necessarily fully measured
Every NULL is a real zero
There can be no unknown state
No matching fact means zero under the reporting policy
questions.explanation: Missing observations and measured zero are distinct unless a policy equates them.

questions.question_text: Four members crossed with themselves produce how many ordered pairs before filtering?
questions.explanation: The complete product includes self-pairs and both directions.

questions.question_text: Which predicate gives unordered distinct-member pairs with unique non-NULL identifiers?
options: a.id = b.id
a.id < b.id
a.id <= b.id
No predicate
questions.explanation: Strict ordering removes self-pairs and retains one direction of each pair.

questions.question_text: Can local Cartesian multiplication occur even when JOIN predicates exist?
options: No, only CROSS JOIN can multiply
No, primary keys prevent every multiplication
Yes, joining two independent one-to-many sources can multiply facts
Only when both tables are empty
questions.explanation: Item-tag combinations can repeat each item once per tag.

questions.question_text: Does writing CROSS JOIN prove a full intermediate product is materialized?
options: Yes, always
Only with integer identifiers
Only with an ORDER BY
No, physical execution is optimizer-dependent
questions.explanation: Logical semantics do not fix the physical plan.

questions.question_text: Why bound requested dimensions before exposing a combination report?
options: Result sizes multiply and can consume substantial resources
CROSS JOIN changes stored rows
Indexes prohibit large products
The output is always unique
questions.explanation: A reasonable plan does not remove the cost of an enormous requested output.

coding_problems.title: List format-slot combinations
coding_problems.task: Return format_id,slot_id for every pair ordered by format_id,slot_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE formats(format_id INT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE slots(slot_id INT PRIMARY KEY);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO formats VALUES (1),(2); INSERT INTO slots VALUES (10),(20);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT f.format_id,s.slot_id FROM formats AS f CROSS JOIN slots AS s ORDER BY f.format_id,s.slot_id;
coding_problems.explanation: Each format pairs with both slots.
coding_problems.ordering: Apply the ORDER BY explicitly required by the task; scalar results contain one row.
constraints: Only synthetic fixture tables are in scope.
edge_cases: Check empty input and the supplied contrasting fixtures.
hints: Each format pairs with both slots.

coding_problems.title: Generate unordered member pairs
coding_problems.task: Return first_id,second_id for each pair of different members once, with first_id<second_id, ordered by both identifiers.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE members(member_id INT PRIMARY KEY);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT a.member_id AS first_id,b.member_id AS second_id FROM members AS a CROSS JOIN members AS b WHERE a.member_id<b.member_id ORDER BY first_id,second_id;
coding_problems.explanation: Strict identity ordering excludes self-pairs and reverse duplicates.
